content: Critical care nursing is a specialized field of nursing that focuses on providing care to critically ill or unstable patients. These nurses work in various settings, including emergency departments and intensive care units (ICUs). Most critical care nurses are registered nurses (RNs), as the complexity and instability of the patient population often make it unsuitable for licensed practical nurses (LPNs) or licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) to serve in primary care roles within ICUs. However, with appropriate training and experience, LPNs/LVNs can contribute significantly by delivering high-quality bedside care to critically ill patients. In the United States, nurses who wish to obtain certification in critical care nursing can do so through the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses (AACN), a national advisory board that establishes and maintains standards for critical care nursing. The certification offered by the AACN is known as CCRN, which does not stand for Critical Care Registered Nurse as commonly believed, but rather signifies certification in critical care nursing for adult, pediatric, and neonatal populations. Registration, on the other hand, is a regulatory process between the nurse and the state in which they practice. All nurses in the U.S. are registered as general nurses without a specialty. The CCRN is an example of a post-registration specialty certification in critical care. The AACN also offers other certifications, such as the PCCN (Progressive Care Certified Nurse), CMC (Cardiac Medicine Certification), and CSC (Cardiac Surgery Certification). Additionally, Clinical Nurse Specialists (CNSs) can obtain certifications in adult, neonatal, and pediatric acute and critical care (CCNS). In November 2007, the AACN Certification Corporation introduced the ACNPC (Acute Care Nurse Practitioner Certification), an advanced practice certification exam for Acute Care Nurse Practitioners. However, none of these certifications grant additional practice privileges, as nursing practice is regulated by individual state boards of nursing. While these certifications are not mandatory for working in an ICU, they are encouraged by employers because they demonstrate a nurse's expertise and commitment to advancing their knowledge and skills in critical care. The certification exams are challenging, requiring extensive knowledge of pathophysiology and critical care practices, and are regarded as a mark of excellence in the field. Critical care nurses must also be proficient in using a wide range of advanced medical technologies commonly employed in critical care settings. These include hemodynamic and cardiac monitoring systems, mechanical ventilators, intra-aortic balloon pumps (IABPs), ventricular assist devices (LVADs and RVADs), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT/CVVHDF), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) circuits, and other life-support devices. Training for these technologies is provided through in-hospital in-services, manufacturer training, and hands-on education with experienced operators. Many employers also ensure that nurses' skills remain up-to-date by sending them to conferences and providing ongoing education to keep pace with rapidly evolving technologies. Critical care nurses work in diverse environments and care for a wide range of patient populations. Many are employed in hospital ICUs, post-operative care units, and high-dependency units. Others work on medical evacuation and transport teams. For example, in 2004, Massachusetts General Hospital invited journalists from The Boston Globe to shadow critical care nurses in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU) for eight months. This immersion experience resulted in a four-part series titled Critical Care: The Making of an ICU Nurse, which highlighted the demanding and skilled nature of critical care nursing. Subspecialties within critical care nursing include Neonatal Intensive Care (NICU), Pediatric Intensive Care (PICU), and Adult Intensive Care (ICU). The patient population in these units is generally determined by age. The NICU primarily cares for newborns and premature infants, typically up to one month old, based on gestational age. After this period, care is usually transferred to the PICU, which manages patients from about one month to 18 years of age. Patients older than 18 are generally admitted to adult ICUs. However, admissions are often determined on a case-by-case basis. For instance, a newborn admitted from the emergency department may be placed in the PICU rather than the NICU, and a 17-year-old weighing 235 pounds may be admitted to an adult ICU. Rarely, adult patients with congenital heart defects may be admitted to the PICU if their physicians have been treating them since childhood and are familiar with their specific conditions and treatment plans. Further subspecialties in critical care nursing are often based on the primary condition or injury of the patient population. For example, an Adult Trauma Intensive Care Unit specializes in the care of trauma patients. The focus of these units is typically on either adult or pediatric/neonatal populations, as treatment methods differ significantly between age groups.
